extracted.intended_audience: general readers and students of 17th-century English religious history and biography (readers of John Bunyan's life)
extracted.subtask_description: A biographical and historical narrative describing John Bunyan's theology, pastoral practice, arrest, trial, and imprisonment in Restoration England. Contains theological positions, pastoral prescriptions, and descriptions of legal procedures and prison conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prayer must be the expression of an inward feeling
rubrics_metrics.description: 'to be worth anything prayer must be the expression of an inward feeling; and that people cannot feel in lines laid down for them.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Forms of prayer (set liturgies) are criticised as ineffective; Bunyan thought forms especially mischievous to children because they accustom them to use words without meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to teach children to pray (method)
rubrics_metrics.description: Teach children early of their sinful condition, the nature of God's wrath and the duration of misery so that conviction of sin will lead them to pray: 'The way that men learn to pray is by conviction of sin, and this is the way to make our "sweet babes" do so too.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bunyan recommends inculcating a strong sense of personal guilt/need as the path to true prayer rather than rote formulas. The text also cautions that such stern teaching risks being 'unreal' or beyond a child's comprehension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid teaching children doctrines they cannot comprehend
rubrics_metrics.description: Warning that teaching doctrines (e.g., metaphysical explanations of wrath and eternal punishment) to children can make them 'unreal' or unable to acknowledge justice of such doctrines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While acknowledging some doctrines may be true, the author suggests care in presenting them to children; moral emotions like 'wrath' belong to free-will contexts and are senseless if applied to unavoidable actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parental conduct in chastisement
rubrics_metrics.description: Parents should 'Take heed that the misdeeds for which thou correctest thy children be not learned them by thee' and avoid encouraging faults by smiling; avoid 'unsavoury and unseemly words' in chastising; do not mix 'many chiding words and threatenings' with lightness and laughter because 'This will harden.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mix mercies with loving rebukes and show 'fatherly and motherly compassions' — loving discipline is more likely to save a child than churlish severity. Even if it does not 'save' them, parents will have comfort that they did their best.

rubrics_metrics.name: Masters' duties toward servants
rubrics_metrics.description: Masters should so behave toward their servants 'that thy service may not only be for thy good, but for the good of thy servant, and that in body and soul.' They should admonish them as with children, not overcharge them with work, not make them into slaves, forbear threatening, and give just labour and just wages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Servants truly godly may serve cheaply to get into godly families, but masters who 'make a prey of their servants' are 'abominable' and make religion 'stink' before others. Practical examples and admonitions are given.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid pride among professing Christians (Professors)
rubrics_metrics.description: Criticism that 'No sin... reigneth more in the world than pride among Professors' and censure of ostentatious apparel and carriage among church members.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-patterns include gaudy garments and excessive adornment; humility and moderation in dress and manner are expected of professing Christians.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conduct for sufferers under persecution toward magistrates
rubrics_metrics.description: Admonition: 'Take heed of being offended with magistrates... it is thy duty to fear him and to pray for him; to give thanks to God for him and be subject to him... not only for wrath, but for conscience sake.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid public discontent or offensive speech (which could lead to severe penalties); practice meekness and patience even when statutes cross inclinations. Discontent in mouth may lead to grave consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal penalties under the 35th of Elizabeth for nonconformity
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the 35th of Elizabeth, Nonconformists refusing to attend parish worship were to be imprisoned till submission; three months were allowed for consideration, after which obstinacy meant banishment from the realm; returning without permission could lead to execution as felons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is presented as the statutory framework used at the Restoration to justify imprisonment and suppression of conventicles; historical context and rationale (fear of sedition) are given.

rubrics_metrics.name: Magistrates' practical handling of Nonconformists (leniency via promises)
rubrics_metrics.description: Magistrates often offered to accept vague promises (e.g., that the accused 'would not call the people together any more') or bail conditioned on not preaching publicly, as a way to avoid harsher punishment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text warns such forms can be intentionally ambiguous; Bunyan refused to accept evasive wording, seeing it as a trap that might allow him to act without conscience restraint. Illustrates tension between legal formality and conscience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two lawful responses to an unjust law
rubrics_metrics.description: Principle: 'The law had provided two ways of obeying--one to obey actively, and if he could not in conscience obey actively, then to suffer whatever penalty was inflicted on him.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This frames Bunyan's choice to endure punishment rather than give up public preaching; presents a moral-legal standard for conscientious dissent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards of historical evidence vs sensational narrative about prison conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Skeptical stance toward embellished descriptions of Bunyan's gaol (e.g., 'damp and dreary cell', 'humid earth', children starving) noting lack of evidence and that wealthy supporters could afford better conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical judgments should be based on evidence (e.g., records of three different gaols, reports of visitors, support from local gentry) rather than sensational imagination; warns against accepting romanticized martyrdom accounts without corroboration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Court procedure and formality in Bunyan's case
rubrics_metrics.description: Bunyan was 'not required to plead' and his 'trial had been a conversation between himself and the Court'; magistrates sometimes treated the matter as capable of informal resolution rather than full trial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The narrative highlights informal judicial practice (conversation, warnings, offers of leniency) and the legal options available (pardon, writ of error); it signals that legal formality could be sidestepped in practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preaching as moral duty not to be limited by numbers
rubrics_metrics.description: Bunyan's assertion: if it is lawful to 'do good to a few, it must be equally lawful to do good to many' — he refused to promise not to call meetings, arguing that presence of people knowing he would speak equates to calling them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This criterion reflects a standard of pastoral conscience that prioritizes use of one's gift to do public good over legal restraints based on crowd size or formal prohibition.
